359: A ≈ 5 µm lumen: red cells squeeze through one by one. Endothelial cells are sealed by continuous tight junctions (claudin-5, occludin), with no fenestrae and very little non-specific transcytosis. Nothing gets through without a transporter — GLUT1 for glucose, LAT1 for large amino acids, MCT1 for lactate and ketone bodies — and efflux pumps (P-glycoprotein) push many drugs back. In the cortex no neuron is more than a few tens of micrometres from a capillary. To cross: the transcytosis point (golden ring).
361: The brain (≈ 2 % of body weight) receives ≈ 15 % of cardiac output and uses ≈ 20 % of the oxygen. Neuronal activity locally dilates vessels (neurovascular coupling): this is the signal measured by functional MRI. The wall can only be crossed by transcytosis (golden ring, ◎ marker). The “Travel by blood” button takes you to another organ.
363: Brain endothelium carries many TfR1 receptors (golden beads): this is how iron enters the brain. Blood transferrin is internalised there in vesicles, and antibodies against TfR1 (“brain shuttles”) use this route to deliver drugs. The fate of transferrin itself — complete crossing, or release of iron in the endosome — is still debated. Disguised as a holo-transferrin, the ship can cross here.
365: A mural cell embedded in the capillary basal lamina, which it grips with its processes. Recruited by endothelial PDGF-B (receptor PDGFRβ), it is essential for the tightness of the blood–brain barrier and helps tune local blood flow.
367: The widened tip of an astrocyte process, pressed onto the capillary: together the endfeet (green plates) cover almost its whole surface. Very rich in aquaporin-4 (water) and Kir4.1 channels (K⁺), they form the interface between blood and nervous tissue.
368: A star-shaped glial cell (GFAP filaments). Each astrocyte occupies its own territory, where it wraps tens of thousands of synapses — far more in humans — and touches vessels with its endfeet. It takes up glutamate (transporters GLT-1 and GLAST) and converts it into glutamine, returned to neurons; it buffers K⁺, stores glycogen, and its calcium signals modulate synapses and blood flow. Astrocytes are coupled to one another by gap junctions (connexin 43).
370: A thin astrocyte sheet apposed to the synapse: with the bouton and the spine it forms the “tripartite synapse”. Its GLT-1 transporters remove glutamate from the cleft within milliseconds, which ends the signal and prevents toxicity; glutamine synthetase converts it into glutamine, which the neuron takes back to remake glutamate.
371: The glial cell that makes central nervous system myelin. Each of its processes wraps its membrane in a spiral around an axon; a single oligodendrocyte thus myelinates up to several dozen segments, on different axons (in nerves, a Schwann cell makes only one). It also supports axonal metabolism by supplying lactate. It is the target of multiple sclerosis.
373: A tight stack of oligodendrocyte membranes, poor in water, rich in lipids (cholesterol, galactocerebroside) and in the proteins PLP and MBP. An electrical insulator: it raises membrane resistance and lowers its capacitance, so the action potential jumps from one node to the next (saltatory conduction), faster and for less energy.
375: A bare axon segment, ≈ 1 µm long, between two internodes. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (Nav1.6) are concentrated there at more than 1,000 per µm², anchored by ankyrin G; Kv1 K⁺ channels are relegated under the myelin on either side (juxtaparanodal regions). The action potential is regenerated here.
376: The resident macrophage of the nervous system, derived from yolk sac precursors and maintained in place (it depends on the CSF1R receptor). Its highly motile processes constantly probe the tissue; attracted by ATP and ADP from injured cells (P2Y12 receptor), they converge within minutes. It removes debris and synapses tagged by complement (C1q, C3), notably during development.
378: The human cerebral cortex has ≈ 16 billion neurons; ≈ 80 % are excitatory pyramidal neurons (glutamate), whose apical dendrite rises towards the surface. Each receives thousands of synapses and makes as many.
380: ≈ 20 % of cortical neurons release GABA. This fast-spiking one (parvalbumin) wraps the soma of pyramidal neurons with its boutons: placed right next to the axon initial segment, this inhibition controls the exact moment the neuron fires and synchronises fast rhythms (gamma oscillations).
382: A GABAergic bouton sitting on the soma. GABA opens GABA-A receptors, Cl⁻-permeable channels anchored by gephyrin: the membrane is held near the chloride equilibrium potential, which opposes depolarisation. A “symmetric” synapse, without a thick postsynaptic density. Benzodiazepines enhance the action of GABA on these receptors.
384: Under the plasma membrane, a felt of actin filaments (7 nm in diameter; a double helix of monomers growing mostly at its “+” end) gives the cell its shape and tension. The Arp2/3 complex starts branches at 70°, formins make straight filaments; myosin II puts it under tension; ERM proteins (ezrin, radixin, moesin) attach it to the membrane. Only a few filaments are drawn.
385: In the red cell lineage it is reorganised into a skeleton of spectrin and short actin filaments, and an actin–myosin ring takes part in expelling the nucleus.
386: In the hepatocyte it is especially dense around the bile canaliculus, whose contractions it drives.
387: In the neuron, actin forms the skeleton of dendritic spines and periodic rings along the axon.
389: Flexible 10 nm cables, with no polarity and no molecular motor, highly resistant to stretching: strung from the nucleus to the membrane, they spread mechanical stress.
390: In the erythroblast these are vimentin filaments; they disappear during maturation, which may help the nucleus to be expelled.
391: In the hepatocyte these are keratins 8 and 18; their aggregates form the Mallory-Denk bodies seen in alcoholic hepatitis and steatohepatitis.
392: In the neuron these are neurofilaments (NF-L, NF-M, NF-H and α-internexin), which extend into the axon and set its calibre.
394: The protein shredder of the cytosol and nucleus (≈ 2.5 MDa, ≈ 45 nm long). The 20S core is a barrel of four rings of seven subunits (α7β7β7α7) whose chamber carries three proteolytic activities (subunits β1, β2 and β5). The 19S caps recognise proteins tagged with a chain of ubiquitins linked through lysine 48, unfold them with six ATPases and thread them into the core, which chops them into peptides of 3 to 25 amino acids. Target of bortezomib, used in myeloma.
395: A spherical shell of 24 H (ferroxidase activity) and L subunits, 12 nm in diameter, whose cavity can store up to ≈ 4,500 iron atoms in mineral form (Fe³⁺). A mobilisable reserve: ferritin is delivered to the lysosome by the autophagy receptor NCOA4 (ferritinophagy). Its translation is blocked by IRP proteins when iron is scarce (IRE element in the 5′UTR of its mRNA).
